claim: Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) is a 42-amino acid peptide hormone that plays crucial role in glucose regulation and fatty acid metabolism.
source: Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) is a 42-amino acid peptide hormone that plays crucial role in glucose regulation and fatty acid metabolism.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about GIP supported by scientific consensus.

claim: In response to food intake, GIP is secreted by intestinal K cells to enhance insulin secretion and peripheral fatty acid uptake.
source: In response to food intake, GIP is secreted by intestinal K cells to enhance insulin secretion and peripheral fatty acid uptake (Kim et al., 2007), as well as a number of neuronal effects (Faivre and Hölscher, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2007 and Faivre and Hölscher, 2013.

claim: GIP has neuronal effects.
source: In response to food intake, GIP is secreted by intestinal K cells to enhance insulin secretion and peripheral fatty acid uptake (Kim et al., 2007), as well as a number of neuronal effects (Faivre and Hölscher, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Faivre and Hölscher, 2013.

claim: The pleiotropic functions of GIP are mediated by its cognate receptor (GIPR), a member of class B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: The pleiotropic functions of GIP is mediated by its cognate receptor (GIPR), a member of class B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that also include glucagon receptor (GCGR) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GIPR classification.

claim: Class B1 GPCRs include glucagon receptor (GCGR) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R).
source: The pleiotropic functions of GIP is mediated by its cognate receptor (GIPR), a member of class B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that also include glucagon receptor (GCGR) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R).
evidence: This is established knowledge about class B1 GPCR classification.

claim: GIPR, together with GCGR and GLP-1R, forms the central endocrine network in regulating insulin sensitivity and energy homeostasis.
source: GIPR, together with GCGR and GLP-1R, forms the central endocrine network in regulating insulin sensitivity and energy homeostasis, and they are validated drug targets (Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008; Finan et al., 2016; Longuet et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008; Finan et al., 2016; Longuet et al., 2008.

claim: GIPR, GCGR, and GLP-1R are validated drug targets.
source: GIPR, together with GCGR and GLP-1R, forms the central endocrine network in regulating insulin sensitivity and energy homeostasis, and they are validated drug targets (Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008; Finan et al., 2016; Longuet et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lagerström and Schiöth, 2008; Finan et al., 2016; Longuet et al., 2008.

claim: A number of GLP-1R selective ligands have been developed successfully to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.
source: A number of GLP-1R selective ligands have been developed successfully to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GLP-1R drug development.

claim: Peptide ligands that bind both GIPR and GLP-1R show better clinical efficacy than the GLP-1R agonist alone.
source: Encouragingly, peptide ligands that bind both GIPR and GLP-1R show better clinical efficacy than the GLP-1R agonist alone.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on clinical observations.

claim: GIPR contains a large extracellular domain (ECD) and a 7-transmembrane domain (TMD).
source: GIPR contains a large extracellular domain (ECD) and a 7-transmembrane domain (TMD).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about GIPR.

claim: Both the ECD and TMD of GIPR are involved in ligand recognition and receptor activation.
source: Both are involved in ligand recognition and receptor activation (Parthier et al., 2009; Koth et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Parthier et al., 2009; Koth et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GCGR and GLP-1R have been solved.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GCGR and GLP-1R, as well as several other class B1 GPCRs have been solved, providing a general mechanism of two-domain model for peptide recognition and receptor activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of class B1 GPCRs provide a general mechanism of two-domain model for peptide recognition and receptor activation.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GCGR and GLP-1R, as well as several other class B1 GPCRs have been solved, providing a general mechanism of two-domain model for peptide recognition and receptor activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the solved structures of multiple class B1 GPCRs.

claim: GIP displays an exquisite sequence specificity towards GIPR as it does not bind to other class B1 GPCRs.
source: However, GIP displays an exquisite sequence specificity towards GIPR as it does not bind to other class B1 GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about GIP binding specificity.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the human GIPR in complex with GIP and a Gs heterotrimer was determined at a global resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the human GIPR in complex with GIP and a Gs heterotrimer at a global resolution of 2.9 Å.
evidence: This is the primary experimental result of the study, supported by the cryo-EM data presented.

claim: GIP adopts a single straight helix with its N terminus dipped into the receptor transmembrane domain (TMD).
source: GIP adopts a single straight helix with its N terminus dipped into the receptor transmembrane domain (TMD), while the C terminus is closely associated with the extracellular domain and extracellular loop 1.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The C terminus of GIP is closely associated with the extracellular domain and extracellular loop 1 of GIPR.
source: GIP adopts a single straight helix with its N terminus dipped into the receptor transmembrane domain (TMD), while the C terminus is closely associated with the extracellular domain and extracellular loop 1.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: GIPR employs conserved residues in the lower half of the TMD pocket to recognize the common segments shared by GIP homologous peptides.
source: GIPR employs conserved residues in the lower half of the TMD pocket to recognize the common segments shared by GIP homologous peptides, while uses non-conserved residues in the upper half of the TMD pocket to interact with residues specific for GIP.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and comparison with homologous receptors.

claim: GIPR uses non-conserved residues in the upper half of the TMD pocket to interact with residues specific for GIP.
source: GIPR employs conserved residues in the lower half of the TMD pocket to recognize the common segments shared by GIP homologous peptides, while uses non-conserved residues in the upper half of the TMD pocket to interact with residues specific for GIP.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and comparison with homologous receptors.

claim: The T345F mutation does not affect the ligand binding or potency of GIP1-42 in cAMP accumulation assay.
source: This mutation does not affect the ligand binding or potency of GIP1-42 in cAMP accumulation assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: The activity of the modified GIPR construct was confirmed by cAMP accumulation assay showing a response similar to that of the wild-type.
source: The activity of the modified GIPR construct was confirmed by cAMP accumulation assay showing a response similar to that of the wild-type (WT; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A total of 295,021 particles were selected after 3D refinement and polishing, leading to an overall resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: A total of 295,021 particles were selected after 3D refinement and polishing, leading to an overall resolution of 2.9 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D and Table 1).
evidence: This is the result of cryo-EM data processing.

claim: Apart from the α-helical domain (AHD) of Gαs which is flexible in most cryo-EM GPCR–G protein complex structures, the bound GIP1-42, GIPR, and Gs were well defined in the EM density maps.
source: Apart from the α-helical domain (AHD) of Gαs which is flexible in most cryo-EM GPCR–G protein complex structures, the bound GIP1-42, GIPR, and Gs were well defined in the EM density maps (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: The final model contains 30 GIP1-42 residues, the Gαβγ subunits of Gs, and the GIPR residues from Q30ECD to S4158.66b.
source: The final model contains 30 GIP1-42 residues, the Gαβγ subunits of Gs, and the GIPR residues from Q30ECD to S4158.66b (class B GPCR numbering in superscript) (Wootten et al., 2013), with six amino acid residues missing at helix 8.
evidence: This describes the content of the final structural model.

claim: Six amino acid residues are missing at helix 8 in the final model.
source: The final model contains 30 GIP1-42 residues, the Gαβγ subunits of Gs, and the GIPR residues from Q30ECD to S4158.66b (class B GPCR numbering in superscript) (Wootten et al., 2013), with six amino acid residues missing at helix 8.
evidence: This describes the content of the final structural model.

claim: The density of ECD is relatively poor owing to its intrinsic flexibility.
source: As a general feature in most reported class B1 GPCR–Gs complex structures (Qiao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2017a; Zhao et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020), the density of ECD is relatively poor owning to its intrinsic flexibility, which limited the accuracy in model building for the GIPR ECD region compared to other regions of the complex structure.
evidence: This is a common observation in class B1 GPCR structures, supported by citations.

claim: Notable conformation difference from GCGR or GLP-1R was observed in the extracellular loop 1 (ECL1).
source: Notable conformation difference from GCGR (Qiao et al., 2020) or GLP-1R (Zhang et al., 2017a) was observed in the extracellular loop 1 (ECL1).
evidence: This is observed through structural comparison.

claim: Y1P of GIP points to TMs 2–3 and forms hydrogen bonds with R1902.67b and Q2243.37b.
source: Y1P (P indicates that the residue belongs to the peptide ligand) of GIP points to TMs 2–3, forms hydrogen bonds with R1902.67b and Q2243.37b, and makes hydrophobic contacts with V2273.40b and W2965.36b.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Y1P of GIP makes hydrophobic contacts with V2273.40b and W2965.36b.
source: Y1P (P indicates that the residue belongs to the peptide ligand) of GIP points to TMs 2–3, forms hydrogen bonds with R1902.67b and Q2243.37b, and makes hydrophobic contacts with V2273.40b and W2965.36b.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mutant W296A decreased the potency of GIP-induced cAMP signaling by 50-fold.
source: This observation received support of the mutagenesis study, where mutant W296A decreased the potency of GIP-induced cAMP signaling by 50-fold (Figure 2D), and the reductions in mutants R190A and Q224A were 71- and 5-fold, respectively, as reported in a previous report (Yaqub et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutant R190A decreased the potency of GIP-induced cAMP signaling by 71-fold.
source: This observation received support of the mutagenesis study, where mutant W296A decreased the potency of GIP-induced cAMP signaling by 50-fold (Figure 2D), and the reductions in mutants R190A and Q224A were 71- and 5-fold, respectively, as reported in a previous report (Yaqub et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yaqub et al., 2010.

claim: Mutant Q224A decreased the potency of GIP-induced cAMP signaling by 5-fold.
source: This observation received support of the mutagenesis study, where mutant W296A decreased the potency of GIP-induced cAMP signaling by 50-fold (Figure 2D), and the reductions in mutants R190A and Q224A were 71- and 5-fold, respectively, as reported in a previous report (Yaqub et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yaqub et al., 2010.

claim: N-terminal truncation of either Y1P or both Y1P and A2P led to reduced efficacy or loss of activity.
source: N-terminal truncation of either Y1P or both Y1P and A2P led to reduced efficacy or loss of activity (Kerr et al., 2011; Gabe et al., 2020), highlighting a crucial role of Y1P.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2011; Gabe et al., 2020.

claim: E3P, D9P, and D15P are three negatively charged residues in the N-terminal half of GIP and form salt bridges with R1832.60b, R3707.35b, and R289ECL2, respectively.
source: E3P, D9P, and D15P are three negatively charged residues in the N-terminal half of GIP and form salt bridges with R1832.60b, R3707.35b, and R289ECL2, respectively.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Removal of salt bridges by alanine substitution at R1832.60b greatly reduced GIP potency by 76-fold.
source: Removal of these salt bridges by alanine substitution at either R1832.60b (Yaqub et al., 2010) or R3707.35b (Figure 2D) greatly reduced GIP potency (by 76- and 55-fold, respectively), whereas the effect on mutant R289A was mild (6-fold, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yaqub et al., 2010.

claim: Removal of salt bridges by alanine substitution at R3707.35b greatly reduced GIP potency by 55-fold.
source: Removal of these salt bridges by alanine substitution at either R1832.60b (Yaqub et al., 2010) or R3707.35b (Figure 2D) greatly reduced GIP potency (by 76- and 55-fold, respectively), whereas the effect on mutant R289A was mild (6-fold, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The effect on mutant R289A was mild (6-fold reduction in GIP potency).
source: Removal of these salt bridges by alanine substitution at either R1832.60b (Yaqub et al., 2010) or R3707.35b (Figure 2D) greatly reduced GIP potency (by 76- and 55-fold, respectively), whereas the effect on mutant R289A was mild (6-fold, Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Polar interactions occurred between S8P and N290ECL2 as well as Y10P and Q1381.40b.
source: Polar interactions also occurred between S8P and N290ECL2 as well as Y10P and Q1381.40b.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The GIP–TMD interface was stabilized by a complementary nonpolar network involving TM1 (L1341.36b, L1371.39b, and Y1411.43b) and TM7 (L3747.39b and I3787.43b) via A2P, F6P, and Y10P of GIP.
source: The GIP–TMD interface was further stabilized by a complementary nonpolar network involving TM1 (L1341.36b, L1371.39b, and Y1411.43b) and TM7 (L3747.39b and I3787.43b) via A2P, F6P, and Y10P of GIP (Figure 2C), in line with decreased ligand potencies observed in Y141A (by 103-fold), L374A (by 41-fold), and I378A (by 8-fold) mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and supported by mutagenesis data.

claim: Mutant Y141A decreased ligand potency by 103-fold.
source: The GIP–TMD interface was further stabilized by a complementary nonpolar network involving TM1 (L1341.36b, L1371.39b, and Y1411.43b) and TM7 (L3747.39b and I3787.43b) via A2P, F6P, and Y10P of GIP (Figure 2C), in line with decreased ligand potencies observed in Y141A (by 103-fold), L374A (by 41-fold), and I378A (by 8-fold) mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutant L374A decreased ligand potency by 41-fold.
source: The GIP–TMD interface was further stabilized by a complementary nonpolar network involving TM1 (L1341.36b, L1371.39b, and Y1411.43b) and TM7 (L3747.39b and I3787.43b) via A2P, F6P, and Y10P of GIP (Figure 2C), in line with decreased ligand potencies observed in Y141A (by 103-fold), L374A (by 41-fold), and I378A (by 8-fold) mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutant I378A decreased ligand potency by 8-fold.
source: The GIP–TMD interface was further stabilized by a complementary nonpolar network involving TM1 (L1341.36b, L1371.39b, and Y1411.43b) and TM7 (L3747.39b and I3787.43b) via A2P, F6P, and Y10P of GIP (Figure 2C), in line with decreased ligand potencies observed in Y141A (by 103-fold), L374A (by 41-fold), and I378A (by 8-fold) mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The C-terminal half of GIP was clasped by the GIPR ECD, closely resembling the crystal structure of GIP–GIPR ECD (PDB code: 2QKH).
source: The C-terminal half of GIP was clasped by the GIPR ECD, closely resembling the crystal structure of GIP–GIPR ECD (PDB code: 2QKH) (Parthier et al., 2007).
evidence: This is observed through structural comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: The hydrophobic residues (F22P, V23P, L26P, and L27P) in the C-terminal half of GIP occupy a complementary binding groove of the GIPR ECD, consisting of a series of hydrophobic residues (L35, Y36, W39, M67, Y68, Y87, L88, P89, and W90).
source: Consistent with the interaction patterns observed in other class B1 GPCRs (Parthier et al., 2007), the hydrophobic residues (F22P, V23P, L26P, and L27P) in the C-terminal half of GIP occupy a complementary binding groove of the GIPR ECD, consisting of a series of hydrophobic residues (L35, Y36, W39, M67, Y68, Y87, L88, P89, and W90).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Alanine substitutions in W39, D66, and Y68 significantly reduced the potency of GIP.
source: Alanine substitutions in W39, D66, and Y68 significantly reduced the potency of GIP (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Several polar contacts including H18P-Y36 and Q20P-N124 were observed.
source: Besides, several polar contacts including H18P-Y36 and Q20P-N124 were observed.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The ECL1 stands upwards to approach the N-terminal α-helix of ECD and forms hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Y36.
source: Notably, the cryo-EM map suggests that the ECL1 stands upwards to approach the N-terminal α-helix of ECD and forms hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Y36 (Figure 2A,B), resulting in a close contact between TMD and ECD for GIP-bound GIPR (interface area = 571 Å2), significantly larger than that of GLP-1-bound GLP-1R (362 Å2), reinforcing the importance of ECD in GIP recognition.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The interface area between TMD and ECD for GIP-bound GIPR is 571 Å2, significantly larger than that of GLP-1-bound GLP-1R (362 Å2).
source: Notably, the cryo-EM map suggests that the ECL1 stands upwards to approach the N-terminal α-helix of ECD and forms hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Y36 (Figure 2A,B), resulting in a close contact between TMD and ECD for GIP-bound GIPR (interface area = 571 Å2), significantly larger than that of GLP-1-bound GLP-1R (362 Å2), reinforcing the importance of ECD in GIP recognition.
evidence: This is calculated from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: GIPR shares ~50% sequence similarity with GCGR, especially in the TMD region (75%).
source: GIPR shares ~50% sequence similarity with GCGR, especially in the TMD region (75%); thus, GCGR structures published previously provide a good template for the present study (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Qiao et al., 2020; Hilger et al., 2020; Jazayeri et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: The TMD of activated GIPR exhibits a conformation similar to that of GCGR activated by glucagon or ZP3780 (Cα RMSD = 1.2 and 0.7 Å, respectively).
source: It was found the TMD of activated GIPR exhibits a conformation similar to that of GCGR activated by glucagon or ZP3780 (Cα RMSD = 1.2 and 0.7 Å, respectively) (Qiao et al., 2020; Hilger et al., 2020) and distinct from that of GCGR bound by the negative allosteric modulator NNC0640 or partial agonist NNC1702 (Cα RMSD = 4.0 and 3.9 Å, respectively) (Zhang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with GCGR structures.

claim: The TMD of activated GIPR is distinct from that of GCGR bound by the negative allosteric modulator NNC0640 or partial agonist NNC1702 (Cα RMSD = 4.0 and 3.9 Å, respectively).
source: It was found the TMD of activated GIPR exhibits a conformation similar to that of GCGR activated by glucagon or ZP3780 (Cα RMSD = 1.2 and 0.7 Å, respectively) (Qiao et al., 2020; Hilger et al., 2020) and distinct from that of GCGR bound by the negative allosteric modulator NNC0640 or partial agonist NNC1702 (Cα RMSD = 4.0 and 3.9 Å, respectively) (Zhang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with GCGR structures.

claim: Facilitated by Gly7.50b located in the middle of TM7, the extracellular half of TM7 bends towards TM6 by 8.0 Å.
source: Facilitated by Gly7.50b located in the middle of TM7, the extracellular half of TM7 bends towards TM6 by 8.0 Å (measured by Cα atom of Gly7.32b) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The extracellular tip of TM1 was extended by one turn and moved inward by 8.0 Å.
source: Meanwhile, the extracellular tip of TM1 was extended by one turn and moved inward by 8.0 Å (measured by Cα atom of the residues at 1.30b) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The sharp kink in the middle of TM6 led to an outward movement of its intracellular portion measured by Cα atom of R3366.35b (18.9 Å, similar to that of other Gs-coupled class B1 receptors).
source: In the intracellular side, the sharp kink in the middle of TM6 led to an outward movement of its intracellular portion measured by Cα atom of R3366.35b (18.9 Å, similar to that of other Gs-coupled class B1 receptors).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and compared with other structures.

claim: The outward movement of TM6 was accompanied by the movement of the intracellular tip of TM5 toward TM6 by 7.6 Å.
source: This was accompanied by the movement of the intracellular tip of TM5 toward TM6 by 7.6 Å (measured by Cα atom of the residues at 5.67b), thereby creating an intracellular cavity for G protein coupling (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Gs protein is anchored by the α5 helix of Gαs (GαH5), thereby fitting to the cytoplasmic cavity formed by TMs 3, 5, and 6, intracellular loops (ICLs) 1–2 and H8.
source: In our model, Gs protein is anchored by the α5 helix of Gαs (GαH5), thereby fitting to the cytoplasmic cavity formed by TMs 3, 5, and 6, intracellular loops (ICLs) 1–2 and H8 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The GIPR–Gs complex shows a similar receptor–G protein interface as other reported class B1 receptor structures such as GLP-1R, GLP-2R, GCGR, PTH1R, SCTR, and GHRHR, suggesting a common G protein signaling mechanism.
source: In general, the GIPR–Gs complex shows a similar receptor–G protein interface as other reported class B1 receptor structures such as GLP-1R (Zhang et al., 2020), GLP-2R (glucagon-like peptide-2 receptor) (Sun et al., 2020), GCGR (Qiao et al., 2020), PTH1R (Zhao et al., 2019), SCTR (secretin receptor) (Dong et al., 2020), and GHRHR (growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor) (Zhou et al., 2020), suggesting a common G protein signaling mechanism (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison with other class B1 receptor structures.

claim: The hydrophobic residues at the C-terminal of GαH5 (L388GαH5, Y391GαH5, L393GαH5, and L394GαH5) insert into a small hydrophobic pocket formed by Y2403.53b, L2413.54b, L2443.57b, L2453.58b, I3175.58b, I3205.60b, L3215.61b, and L3255.65b.
source: The hydrophobic residues at the C-terminal of GαH5 (L388GαH5, Y391GαH5, L393GαH5, and L394GαH5) insert into a small hydrophobic pocket formed by Y2403.53b, L2413.54b, L2443.57b, L2453.58b, I3175.58b, I3205.60b, L3215.61b, and L3255.65b (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The side chain of R3386.37b points to Gαs and makes one hydrogen bond with L394GαH5.
source: The side chain of R3386.37b points to Gαs and makes one hydrogen bond with L394GαH5.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The interaction between R380GαH5 and ICL2 results in five hydrogen bonds with the backbone atoms of L2453.58b, V2463.59b, L2473.60b, and V248ICL2, significantly more than that observed in GLP-1R, SCTR, or GCGR.
source: Of note is that the interaction between R380GαH5 and ICL2 results in five hydrogen bonds with the backbone atoms of L2453.58b, V2463.59b, L2473.60b, and V248ICL2, significantly more than that observed in GLP-1R, SCTR, or GCGR (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure and compared with other structures.

claim: The polar residues in ICL2 (S251ICL2 and E253ICL2) produce two hydrogen bonds with K34 and Q35 of Gαs.
source: The polar residues in ICL2 (S251ICL2 and E253ICL2) produce two hydrogen bonds with K34 and Q35 of Gαs, while H8 forms several hydrogen bonds with ICL1, then contacts with Gβ (E3988.49b-R164ICL1-D312Gβ, E4028.53b-R164ICL1-D312Gβ) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: H8 forms several hydrogen bonds with ICL1, then contacts with Gβ (E3988.49b-R164ICL1-D312Gβ, E4028.53b-R164ICL1-D312Gβ).
source: The polar residues in ICL2 (S251ICL2 and E253ICL2) produce two hydrogen bonds with K34 and Q35 of Gαs, while H8 forms several hydrogen bonds with ICL1, then contacts with Gβ (E3988.49b-R164ICL1-D312Gβ, E4028.53b-R164ICL1-D312Gβ) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon all adopt a single continuous helix, with the N terminus penetrating to the TMD core to the same depth.
source: Superimposing the TMD of GIP-bound GIPR with that of GLP-1-bound GLP-1R (Zhang et al., 2020) or glucagon-bound GCGR (Qiao et al., 2020) displays a similar ligand-binding pocket and the three peptides all adopt a single continuous helix, with the N terminus penetrating to the TMD core to the same depth, while the C terminus anchors the ECD and ECL1 in a receptor-specific manner (Figure 4).
evidence: This is observed through structural comparison.

claim: The C terminus of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon anchors the ECD and ECL1 in a receptor-specific manner.
source: Superimposing the TMD of GIP-bound GIPR with that of GLP-1-bound GLP-1R (Zhang et al., 2020) or glucagon-bound GCGR (Qiao et al., 2020) displays a similar ligand-binding pocket and the three peptides all adopt a single continuous helix, with the N terminus penetrating to the TMD core to the same depth, while the C terminus anchors the ECD and ECL1 in a receptor-specific manner (Figure 4).
evidence: This is observed through structural comparison.

claim: The ECL1 of GIPR stands upwards in line with TMs 2 and 3 and moves towards the TMD core by 5~7 Å.
source: Notably, the ECL1 of GIPR stands upwards in line with TMs 2 and 3 and moves towards the TMD core by 5~7 Å.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The movement of ECL1, together with a α-helical extension in TM1 by six residues, allows GIP to shift to TM1 by 2.7 and 3.3 Å relative to GLP-1 and glucagon, respectively.
source: Such a movement, together with a α-helical extension in TM1 by six residues, allows GIP to shift to TM1 by 2.7 and 3.3 Å (measured by Cα atom of L27P) relative to GLP-1 (Zhang et al., 2020) and glucagon (Qiao et al., 2020), respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed through structural comparison.

claim: Based on sequence similarity, GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon can be divided into four segments: N terminus (residues 1–3), segment 2 (residues 4–11), segment 3 (residues 12–20), and the C terminus (residues 21 to the end), where segments 2 and 4 are highly conserved.
source: Based on the sequence similarity, the three peptides can be divided into four segments: two common segments (residues 4–11 and 21–30 in GIP) and two unique segments (residues 1–3 and 12–20 in GIP) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: GIPR, GLP-1R, and GCGR employ conserved residues to recognize the common segments of their endogenous peptides and use non-conserved residues to make specific interaction that govern the ligand selectivity.
source: It appears that GIPR, GLP-1R, and GCGR employ conserved residues to recognize the common segments of their endogenous peptides and use non-conserved residues to make specific interaction that govern the ligand selectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and comparison.

claim: GIP modulates glucose metabolism by stimulating the β-cells to release insulin.
source: As one of the incretin hormones, GIP modulates glucose metabolism by stimulating the β-cells to release insulin (Seino et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seino et al., 2010.

claim: Unlike GLP-1, GIP does not suppress gastric emptying and appetite.
source: Unlike GLP-1, it does not suppress gastric emptying and appetite, while exerting opposite actions on pancreatic α-cells as well as adipocytes leading to glucagon secretion and lipogenesis (Seino et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seino et al., 2010.

claim: GIP exerts opposite actions on pancreatic α-cells as well as adipocytes leading to glucagon secretion and lipogenesis.
source: Unlike GLP-1, it does not suppress gastric emptying and appetite, while exerting opposite actions on pancreatic α-cells as well as adipocytes leading to glucagon secretion and lipogenesis (Seino et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seino et al., 2010.

claim: Development of GIPR-based therapeutics met little success due to reduced sensitivity in type 2 diabetic patients.
source: Coupled with reduced sensitivity in type 2 diabetic patients, development of GIPR-based therapeutics met little success (Coskun et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coskun et al., 2018.

claim: Bound peptides (GLP-1, exendin-P5, glucagon, ZP3780, secretin, GHRH, GLP-2, and GIP) in the glucagon subfamily of GPCRs all adopt a single straight helix with their N terminus inserted into the TMD core, while the C-terminal is recognized by the ECD.
source: Comparison of the full-length structures of six glucagon subfamily of GPCRs demonstrates that bound peptides (GLP-1, exendin-P5, glucagon, ZP3780, secretin, GHRH, GLP-2, and GIP) all adopt a single straight helix with their N terminus inserted into the TMD core, while the C-terminal is recognized by the ECD (Zhou et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Qiao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2017a; Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of multiple structures, supported by citations.

claim: For parathyroid hormone subfamily of GPCRs, the long-acting PTH analog (LA-PTH) predominantly exhibits an extended helix with its N terminus inserted deeply into the TMD, where the peptide C terminus may bend occasionally.
source: For parathyroid hormone subfamily of GPCRs, the long-acting PTH analog (LA-PTH) predominantly exhibits an extended helix with its N terminus inserted deeply into the TMD, where the peptide C terminus may bend occasionally (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: In the case of CRF subfamily of GPCRs, the N terminus (first seven residues) of urocortin 1 (UCN1) and CRF1 present an extended loop conformation, and its C-terminal residues (8–40) adopt a single extended helix.
source: In the case of CRF subfamily of GPCRs, the N terminus (first seven residues) of urocortin 1 (UCN1) and CRF1 present an extended loop conformation, and its C-terminal residues (8–40) adopt a single extended helix (Ma et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020.

claim: For calcitonin subfamily of GPCRs, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) has an unstructured loop in both N- and C-terminal regions.
source: As far as calcitonin subfamily of GPCRs is concerned, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) has an unstructured loop in both N- and C-terminal regions (Liang et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2018a.

claim: For PACAP and VIP receptor subfamily, PACAP displays an extended α-helix, while maxadilan, a natural PAC1R agonist (61-amino acid long), forms the N- and C-terminal helices that are linked as a loop.
source: Looking at pituitary adenylate-cyclase-activating peptide (PACAP) and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) receptor subfamily, PACAP displays an extended α-helix, while maxadilan, a natural PAC1R agonist (61-amino acid long), forms the N- and C-terminal helices that are linked as a loop (Duan et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duan et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Human GIP is a comparatively weak partial agonist in rodent models.
source: Indeed, a previous study found that human GIP is a comparatively weak partial agonist in rodent models (Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016.

claim: Human (Pro3)GIP is a full agonist with identical maximum response as human GIP.
source: Human (Pro3)GIP is a full agonist with identical maximum response as human GIP, whereas both rat and mouse (Pro3)GIPs are partial agonists (Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016; Bailey, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016; Bailey, 2020.

claim: Both rat and mouse (Pro3)GIPs are partial agonists.

evidence: Supported by citations to Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016; Bailey, 2020.

claim: Among rat, mouse, and human GIPs, the only residue change (from His to Arg) occurs at the 18th position.
source: Of note is that among rat, mouse, and human GIPs, the only residue change (from His to Arg) occurs at the 18th position (Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sparre-Ulrich et al., 2016.

claim: GIP1-42 and GLP-1 specifically activate GIPR and GLP-1R, respectively.
source: This property is consistent with their behavior in inducing cAMP responses: GIP1-42 and GLP-1 specifically activate GIPR and GLP-1R, respectively, whereas glucagon can elicit cAMP accumulation mediated by both GCGR and GLP-1R (EC50 = 1.14 nM; Figure 4—figure supplement 4), highlighting the complexity of their interactive functionalities.
evidence: This is observed in functional assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Glucagon can elicit cAMP accumulation mediated by both GCGR and GLP-1R (EC50 = 1.14 nM).
source: This property is consistent with their behavior in inducing cAMP responses: GIP1-42 and GLP-1 specifically activate GIPR and GLP-1R, respectively, whereas glucagon can elicit cAMP accumulation mediated by both GCGR and GLP-1R (EC50 = 1.14 nM; Figure 4—figure supplement 4), highlighting the complexity of their interactive functionalities.
evidence: This is observed in functional assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.
